Floating-point addition is not associative because modern computers represent real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, the expressions (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) always have the same value. In floating-point arithmetic, however, each intermediate result is usually rounded to the nearest representable number. Changing the grouping changes which intermediate values are rounded, so the final answers can differ.

For example, suppose a is a very large positive number, b is the corresponding large negative number, and c is a comparatively small number. Computing a + b first may produce zero, after which adding c yields c. Computing b + c first may cause c to be lost because it is too small to affect b at the available precision. Adding a afterward may then produce zero. Neither behavior violates the floating-point standard; it is a consequence of limited significand bits and the large variation in representable magnitudes.

Large matrix multiplications expose this issue because each output element is a dot product, formed by multiplying many pairs of entries and summing the products. Sequential software might accumulate these products from left to right. High-performance implementations instead divide them among vector lanes, processor cores, GPU threads, or distributed machines. Each worker computes a partial sum, and those partial sums are combined through a reduction tree. Different thread counts, block sizes, scheduling decisions, library algorithms, or hardware architectures can produce different reduction trees and therefore different rounding sequences.

Further variation can arise from fused multiply-add instructions, which compute a product and addition with a single final rounding rather than rounding the product and sum separately. GPUs and specialized matrix units may also use different internal precisions or accumulation modes. Consequently, two implementations using the same input matrices can return results that differ in their low-order bits. If scheduling or reduction behavior is nondeterministic, repeated runs on the same system may also differ slightly.

These discrepancies are usually small relative to the scale of the result, but they can matter. They may cause exact equality tests or checksums to fail, alter threshold-based decisions, and accumulate through later numerical computations. Algorithms that are ill-conditioned can amplify tiny changes substantially.

Reproducibility therefore requires more than fixing the inputs and random seeds. It may require a deterministic reduction order, fixed thread configuration, consistent compiler and library settings, controlled use of fused operations, or reproducible summation methods. Higher-precision accumulation and compensated summation can reduce sensitivity, but often cost performance. In practice, numerical results are usually compared with carefully chosen tolerances rather than requiring bit-for-bit equality.
